back: Pay only for the resources you actually use, as operational expenditure — no up-front hardware purchase, and the bill scales down as well as up.

Duties split between provider and customer. Microsoft always owns the physical infrastructure; you always own your data, devices, and identities; the middle layers shift toward Microsoft from IaaS → PaaS → SaaS.
You supply only code; the platform allocates all infrastructure on demand and bills per execution. Azure Functions is the flagship example.

front: Public vs private vs hybrid cloud
back: Public: provider-owned shared infrastructure. Private: infrastructure dedicated to one organisation — most control, usually most cost. Hybrid: the two combined, e.g. regulated data on-premises with everything else in Azure.
A hybrid pattern where a workload runs on private infrastructure and 'bursts' into public cloud capacity when local resources are exhausted.

front: Pay-as-you-go vs reserved vs spot pricing
back: Pay-as-you-go: highest unit price, total flexibility. Reserved: 1- or 3-year commitment for deep discounts on steady workloads. Spot: deepest discounts for interruptible workloads Azure may evict.
The service keeps responding despite component failures, expressed in uptime SLAs — 99.9% allows ~8.7 hours of downtime a year; 99.99% allows ~52 minutes.
Vertical: make one machine bigger (more CPU/RAM). Horizontal: add more machines. Elasticity is scaling that happens automatically with demand.
The ability to recover from failure and keep functioning — e.g. a decentralised design that shifts work to a healthy region when one fails.

front: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS in one line each
back: IaaS: rent VMs and networks, you manage the OS up (lift-and-shift). PaaS: you bring code and data, provider runs the platform (App Service). SaaS: you use a finished app (Microsoft 365).
IaaS: the customer. PaaS and SaaS: Microsoft. The single most-tested consequence of the shared responsibility model.
A geographic area containing one or more datacenters with low-latency connectivity, where you choose to deploy resources.
A physically separate location within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking — spreading across zones survives a datacenter failure.
Two regions ≥300 miles apart in one geography: replication target, sequenced platform updates, and prioritised recovery after a broad outage.
A physically and logically isolated Azure instance for special compliance jurisdictions — Azure Government, Azure operated by 21Vianet (China).
A mandatory container for resources sharing a lifecycle. Deleting the group deletes its contents; a resource belongs to exactly one group at a time.
The billing and access boundary — costs accumulate per subscription, and organisations commonly split production and development this way.
A container above subscriptions so policy and access apply once and are inherited by every subscription beneath.
Groups of identical VMs with autoscaling and a built-in load balancer — the answer to 'many identical instances that grow with load'.
Spreads VMs across separate power/network hardware (fault domains) and separate maintenance windows (update domains) within one datacenter.
VMs virtualise hardware (full OS control); containers virtualise the OS (lighter, faster); Functions run event-driven code with no server management at all.
Both connect on-premises to Azure. VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnel over the public internet. ExpressRoute: dedicated private circuit that never touches the internet.
Connects two virtual networks — including across regions — so they route to each other as one network.
Public: the service has an internet-reachable address. Private: the service gets a private IP inside your VNet, so traffic never leaves the private network.
Hot: frequent access. Cool/Cold: infrequent access, minimum 30/90-day storage. Archive: cheapest to hold, hours to retrieve — long-term retention.
LRS: 3 copies, one datacenter. ZRS: copies across availability zones. GRS/GZRS: adds a secondary region (RA- variants make it readable). Regional disaster protection starts at GRS.
A rugged physical appliance Microsoft ships to you for offline transfer of very large datasets that would take too long over the network.
AzCopy: command-line transfers. Storage Explorer: the same graphically. Azure File Sync: caches Azure file shares on local Windows servers.
Azure's cloud identity service — authentication for Azure, Microsoft 365, and connected apps. Entra Domain Services adds managed domain join and group policy.
Policy engine that evaluates sign-in signals (location, device, risk) and applies controls — require MFA, or block — before access is granted.

front: Zero Trust vs defense in depth
back: Zero Trust: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach. Defense in depth: layered controls (physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, app, data) so one breach doesn't win.
Pricing calculator: estimates what a planned Azure architecture will cost. TCO calculator: compares current on-premises costs with running in Azure.
Data transferred out of Azure is billed; data transferred in is generally free. Network traffic direction is a classic hidden cost factor.
Name:value metadata on resources (e.g. costcenter:finance) used to organise resources and slice cost reports without restructuring subscriptions.
Microsoft Cost Management lets you set spending thresholds per scope and fires alerts as actual or forecast spend approaches them.
Evaluates resources against rules (allowed regions, SKUs, required tags), blocks non-compliant creations, reports existing violations. Initiatives bundle policies.
Delete lock: blocks deletion. Read-only lock: blocks all changes. Both apply even to owners and must be removed before the guarded action can proceed.
Projects on-premises servers, other clouds, and Kubernetes clusters into Azure Resource Manager so Policy, RBAC, and monitoring govern them like native resources.
Azure Resource Manager is the deployment layer every tool talks to. ARM templates (and Bicep) declare a desired end state — the same file produces the same environment every time.
Advisor: free personalised recommendations (cost, security, reliability, performance, operations). Service Health: Azure incidents, maintenance, and advisories scoped to what you use.

front: Azure Monitor / Log Analytics / Application Insights
back: Monitor: platform-wide metrics and logs pipeline with alerts. Log Analytics: workspace and query engine over collected logs. Application Insights: app-level telemetry — requests, failures, dependencies.
Committing to one or three years of usage in advance for a large discount over pay-as-you-go. The trade is price against flexibility, not a change to the resource itself.
A concise declarative language that compiles to ARM templates. Same deployment engine and same idempotent result, far less JSON to read.
